# Novel Multi Security and Privacy Benchmarking Framework for Blockchain-Based IoT Healthcare Industry 4.0 Systems
Sarah Qahtan, Khaironi Yatim Sharif, A. A. Zaidan , H. A. Alsattar, O. S. Albahri, B. B. Zaidan, Hazura Zulzalil, M. H. Osman, A. H. Alamoodi, and R. T. Mohammed
Abstract—The evaluation, importance and variation nature of multiple security and privacy properties are the main issues that make the benchmarking of blockchainbased IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems fall under the multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) problem. In this article, one of the recent MCDM weighting methods called fuzzy weighted with zero inconsistency (FWZIC) is effective for weighting the evaluation criteria subjectively without any inconsistency issues. However, considering the advantages of spherical fuzzy sets in providing a wide range of options to decision-makers and efficiently dealing with vagueness, hesitancy and uncertainty, this article formulated a new version of FWZIC for weighting the security and privacy properties, that is, spherical FWZIC (S-FWZIC). Moreover, an integrated MCDM framework was developed for benchmarking blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems on the basis of multi security and privacy properties. In the first phase of the methodology, a decision matrix is formulated based on the intersection of "blockchain-based Internet of Things healthcare Industry 4.0 systems" and "security and privacy properties" (i.e.,

In the second phase, the weights of each security and privacy property are calculated through the S-FWZIC method. Then, these weights are employed to benchmark blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems through the combined grey relational analysis-technique for order of preference by similarity to ideal solution (GRA-TOPSIS) and the bald eagle search (BES) optimization method. Results indicate the following: First, the S-FWZIC method efficiently weighs the security and privacy properties, indicating that access control has the highest significance weight of 0.2070, while integrity has the lowest weight (0.0646); and second, the combination of the GRA-TOPSIS and the BES optimization method effectively ranks the systems. The evaluation was conducted using sensitivity analysis, revealing high correlation results over all the discussed scenarios of changing the weights of the criteria. The implications of this article can assist medical organisation administrators in selecting the most secure and appropriate system and the developers of such systems in future directions.
Index Terms—Blockchain, healthcare industry 4.0 systems, security and privacy.
## I. INTRODUCTION
EALTHCARE industry 4.0 is one of the fastest-growing and most prominent industries in the world. However, this industry has faced grave socio-economic issues in many countries over the last decade. Many academics, such as [1] have surveyed and reviewed blockchain technology's impact on healthcare Industry 4.0 and [2]–[4] focused on the significant improvement in privacy, security, data sharing and prevention of unauthorised users through blockchain technology. In this article, the study by [1] identified remote patient monitoring systems (RPMSs) as one of the emerging categories of healthcare systems. With the help of the Internet of Things (IoT), healthcare Industry 4.0 systems (RPMSs in specific) have been notably revolutionized by the efficient transfer of patient data through wireless body area network, biomedical sensors and cloud storage.
According to [1], blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems can be evaluated using many security and privacy properties: user authentication, access control, privacy preservation, integrity, availability and anonymity. However, the literature presents varying views regarding the use of these properties

in blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems. For example, [5] used access control and integrity, while [6] employed authentication, access control, privacy preservation, integrity and availability. Despite all these remarkable efforts, a unified application with all the desirable properties is yet to be presented.
The procedure of determining the most suitable system is complex, but can be addressed by evaluating and benchmarking blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems. A previous work [1] evaluated these systems; nonetheless, no benchmarking report has been presented, which is considered a research gap. The benchmarking of blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems to determine the most secure and private system is crucial and challenging. Despite the numerous systems available in the literature, no superior system meets all vital properties. The different combinations of the security and privacy properties in blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems complicate such a task. Three critical issues are addressed in benchmarking blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems to bridge the identified research gap: multiple evaluation criteria; criteria importance; and data variation. Some criteria were used in the design of blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems in previous studies. Hence, multiple criteria should be considered when benchmarking these designs. The importance of these criteria also varies as studies combine them in various ways [5], [6]. In addition, the availability of such criteria varies in each healthcare Industry 4.0 system, and this variation increases with the complexity of the tasks in each system. Therefore, complex multicriteria decision-making (MCDM) problems will arise when benchmarking blockchainbased IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems on the basis of the aforementioned issues. Therefore, complex MCDM problems will arise when benchmarking blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems on the basis of the aforementioned issues. Thus, an MCDM approach is needed to bridge this gap and solve the problem's complexity.
Several MCDM methods have been developed and applied in different fields, including ranking alternatives and criteria weighing, such as [7]. The technique for order of preference by similarity to ideal solution (TOPSIS) is one of the top ranking methods used by many researchers to determine which alternative is the best or ideal [8], [9]. However, the Euclidean distance applied in the classical TOPSIS method has some shortcomings [10]: distortion of the original information; insensitivity to small values; relatively small distance between the positive and negative ideal solutions; and rank reversal defects. Many improved versions of TOPSIS have been presented in the literature to overcome these flaws. Canberra distance, contact vector distance, hamming distance, M-TOPSIS and generalised hybrid distance have all been proposed as alternatives to Euclidean distance. For the same purpose, other groups of academics integrated grey relational analysis (GRA) with TOPSIS. The GRA method's main benefits include enabling easy and straightforward calculations and the decisions are based on the original information, and the GRA method is one of the most effective methods for making business decisions. In addition, GRA can deal with complex decision-making situations (e.g., incomplete, inaccurate and ambiguous data) [11]. Recently, Liu *et al.* [12] introduced a
hybrid ranking method for evaluating and comparing the daily performance of the electricity market. The method improved GRA-TOPSIS by using an optimization model to find the final closeness between the evaluation sample and the ideal solutions, which is considered an optimization problem. According to [13], the bald eagle search (BES) algorithm outperforms advanced meta-heuristic algorithms and traditional approaches with its introduction of more complex mechanisms and integration of powerful operators with other heuristics. Therefore, the combination of the GRA-TOPSIS and the BES optimization method was adopted in the article to benchmark the healthcare Industry 4.0 system alternatives.
Furthermore, the combined GRA-TOPSIS and BES optimization method cannot weigh the criteria, requiring an external method to accomplish this task [14]. Many studies considered integrating the analytic hierarchy process (AHP) into the combination of the GRA-TOPSIS and the optimization method. The AHP and best–worst method (BWM) approaches have demonstrated a high degree of success in weighting criteria. However, the inconsistency of their weighting methods remains a critical issue [14]. Furthermore, when the relationship and interdependency of high- and low-level elements are considered, many decision issues cannot be organized hierarchically. BWM requires fewer paired comparisons than AHP and produces a higher consistency score to weigh a criterion [15]. The only difficulty with BWM is identifying the best and worst criteria, including the relative importance of all criteria versus the best and worst for specific criteria [16]. Consequently, adopting one of these approaches to evaluate blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems is deemed impractical.
Recently, the fuzzy weighted with zero inconsistency (FWZIC) method was proposed to determine the weight coefficients of criteria with zero inconsistency regardless of their number [17], [18]. The FWZIC method achieves zero inconsistency by individually and precisely computing the local and global weight coefficient values of all the criteria at a given hierarchy level. In addition, the FWZIC method can compute the importance level of each criterion in the decision-making process according to expert preferences. The FWZIC method is deemed the best criteria weighting method for evaluating the security and privacy properties of blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems as it successfully solves the inconsistency issue. However, in the original version of the FWZIC method [17], triangular fuzzy numbers (TFNs) are utilized but make each membership grade input a crisp value. TFNs fail to directly model and mitigate the effects of data uncertainty. The same group of researchers developed a new extension of the FWZIC method using trapezoidal fuzzy numbers (TrFNs) [18]. TrFNs can define the exact membership function, model second-order uncertainties and enable easy calculations. However, TrFNs linearize all intermediate degrees of membership [23], which may be inappropriate when focusing on a certain degree of uncertainty, except for 0 or 1. In MCDM, vagueness, hesitancy and uncertainty issues greatly affect the final score assigned to the alternatives. Typically, these issues originate from the decision makers' opinions. Thus, FWZIC has been presented in papers while being extended in different fuzzy environments,

Furthermore, different fuzzy set theories exist and can be used to define and capture the vagueness, hesitancy and uncertainty of information. SFSs use the nonlinear distance between a degree of membership, nonmembership, and hesitancy, and their sum may be greater than one, but their square sum should be between 0 and 1 [23]. SFSs increase the intelligence (comparable to human decision) of the decision-making process, leading to high accuracy in evaluating the alternatives. Therefore, SFSs are widely used because of their potential to provide decision-makers with a wide range of options for dealing with vagueness, hesitancy and uncertainty more successfully and efficiently than the other methods [24].
The implications of this article can assist medical organization administrators in selecting the most secure and private system and the developers of such systems in designing secure systems.
The following points summarise the study's contributions.
- 1) This article developed a new formulation of the FWZIC method under the spherical fuzzy environment, i.e., spherical FWZIC (S-FWZIC) method. - 2) This article developed a method that combines the GRA-TOPSIS and the BES optimization method. - 3) On the basis of multi security and privacy properties, this article developed a novel MCDM framework on the basis of the integration of S-FWZIC into the combination of the GRA-TOPSIS and the BES optimization method for benchmarking blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems.
The rest of this article is organized as follows. The methodology of benchmarking blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems is proposed in Section II. In Section III, the benchmarked results are presented and discussed. The evaluation of the proposed method is presented in Section IV. Finally, Section V concludes this article.
# II. METHODOLOGY
In this section, the proposed framework used in the benchmarking of blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems is explained based on the two-phase methodology.
# *A. Phase I: Decision Matrix Identification*
In the proposed framework, the decision matrix (DM) is regarded as the primary component designed and implemented to benchmark blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems. The intersection of the evaluation criteria (e.g., the security and privacy properties) and the alternatives is used to showcase the DM, as given in Table I.
This article adopted the blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems from a previous study [1]. Six security and privacy properties in the blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems were identified, namely, access control, user authentication, privacy protection, integrity, availability and anonymity. These properties were evaluated by the previous study [1] and classified as binomial criteria measured by either "Yes = 1" or "No = 0." In this article, 1 and 0, respectively, reflect the existence and absence of the criteria in each system. A DM for blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems is formed as follows based on the identified criteria and alternatives. The DM is created by intersecting alternatives (i.e., the set of blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems) and the security and privacy properties (criteria).
## *B. Phase II: Development*
This section presents the details of the development of the proposed framework used for benchmarking blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems. The following subsections are described in the proposed MCDM framework in detail.
- *1) S-FWZIC Method for Weighting Security and Privacy Cri**teria:* The S-FWZIC method is a new extension of the FWZIC method [17] with SFSs, consisting of the following five basic steps. a) *Step 1. Criteria definition*: The evaluation criteria are defined in this step, while the panel of experts is identified and selected for criteria evaluation in the next step.b) *Step 2. Structured expert judgment* (SEJ): This step identifies and selects specialists in the field of security and privacy of healthcare systems. Then, an evaluation form is developed. This task is a vital step in the data collection from experts. The questionnaire's reliability and validity are tested by the experts selected in the previous step. Then, the level of importance is determined. The experts define the importance/significance level of the criteria by using a five-point Likert scale. Finally, linguistic terms
are converted into equivalent numerical scoring scales, as given in Table II.
- c) Step 3. Building the expert DM (EDM): This step creates an EDM that contains the decision criteria (i.e., security and privacy properties) and alternatives (i.e., blockchainbased IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems). A crossover is established between the security and privacy properties and the SEJ panel. Each criterion is intersected with each selected expert who assigns the importance/significance level to all the criteria. - d) Step 4. Application of a fuzzy membership function: SFS's membership function and subsequent defuzzification process are applied to the EDM data. The result of this step is a SFS EDM that improves the accuracy and simplicity of data for future analysis. However, the MCDM problems are uncertain and imprecise because of the difficulty of assigning a specific preference rate to any given criterion. To overcome these problems, fuzzy methods are used to determine the criteria value using vague numbers rather than crisp numbers [14]. As mentioned, S-FWZIC can overcome inconsistency and achieve high accuracy. The SFS is presented in [26] and expressed in the following equations. SFS \tilde{A}_s of the universe of discourse U is expressed as follows:
$$ \tilde{A}_{s} = \left\{ u, \ \mu_{\tilde{A}_{s}}(u), \ \nu_{\tilde{A}_{s}}(u), \ \pi_{\tilde{A}_{s}}(u) \right\} where \mu_{\tilde{A}_{s}}(u) : U \to [0, 1], \ \nu_{\tilde{A}_{s}}(u) : U \to [0, 1], \pi_{\tilde{A}_{s}}(u) : U \to [0, 1] (1) $$
and
$$ 0 \le \mu_{\tilde{A}_S}^2(u) + v_{\tilde{A}_S}^2(u) + \pi_{\tilde{A}_S}^2(u) \le 1 \forall_u \in U. (2) $$
For each u, \mu_{\tilde{A}_s}(u), \nu_{\tilde{A}_s}(u) and \pi_{\tilde{A}_s}(u) represent the degrees of membership, non-membership and hesitancy of u to \tilde{A}_s, respectively. \chi_{\tilde{A}_s} = (1 - \mu_{\tilde{A}_s}^2(u) - \nu_{\tilde{A}_s}^2(u) - \pi_{\tilde{A}_s}^2(u))^{1/2} represents the refusal degree.
The SFS operations used are represented in the following definitions [26].
Let SFSs be \tilde{A}_s = (\mu_{\tilde{A}_s}, \ \nu_{\tilde{A}_s}, \ \pi_{\tilde{A}_s}) and \tilde{B}_s = (\mu_{\tilde{B}_s}, \ \nu_{\tilde{B}_s}, \ \pi_{\tilde{B}_s}).
Multiplication by a scalar: for \lambda \geq 0
$$ \lambda \cdot \tilde{A}_{s} = \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} \left(1 - \left(1 - \mu_{\tilde{A}_{s}}^{2}\right)^{\lambda}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}, \ \nu_{\tilde{A}_{s}}^{\lambda}, \\ \left(\left(1 - \mu_{\tilde{A}_{s}}^{2}\right)^{\lambda} - \left(1 - \mu_{\tilde{A}_{s}}^{2} - \pi_{\tilde{A}_{s}}^{2}\right)^{\lambda}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}, \\ \left(\left(1 - \mu_{\tilde{A}_{s}}^{2}\right)^{\lambda} - \left(1 - \mu_{\tilde{A}_{s}}^{2} - \pi_{\tilde{A}_{s}}^{2}\right)^{\lambda}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}, \\ (3) $$
Division [27]: if \frac{\mu_{\bar{B}_s}^2}{\mu_{\bar{A}_s}^2} \geq \frac{1-\pi_{\bar{B}_s}^2 1+\pi_{\bar{A}_s}^2}{1-\pi_{\bar{A}_s}^2 1+\pi_{\bar{B}_s}^2} \geq 1
$$ \tilde{A}_{s} \oslash \tilde{B}_{s} = \begin{pmatrix} \left( \frac{(\mu_{\tilde{A}_{s}}^{2}(2-\mu_{\tilde{B}_{s}}^{2})}{1-(1-\mu_{\tilde{A}_{s}}^{2})\cdot(1-\mu_{\tilde{B}_{s}}^{2})} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}}, \frac{(v_{\tilde{A}_{s}}^{2}-v_{\tilde{B}_{s}}^{2})^{\frac{1}{2}}}{(1-v_{\tilde{A}_{s}}^{2}\cdot v_{\tilde{B}_{s}}^{2})^{\frac{1}{2}}}, \\ \frac{(\pi_{\tilde{A}_{s}}^{2}\cdot\pi_{\tilde{B}_{s}}^{2})^{\frac{1}{2}}}{(1-\pi_{\tilde{A}_{s}}^{2}\cdot\pi_{\tilde{B}_{s}}^{2})^{\frac{1}{2}}} \end{pmatrix}. \tag{4} $$
The same group of authors defined the spherical weighted arithmetic mean (SWAM) for SFS with respect to w =
$$ (w_1, w_2..., w_n); w_i \in [01]; \sum_{i=1}^n w_i = 1 $$
SWAM_w(\tilde{A}_{S1}, \dots, \tilde{A}_{Sn}) = w_1 \tilde{A}_{S1} + w_1 \tilde{A}_{S1} + \dots + w_n \tilde{A}_{Sn}
$$ = \left\{ \left[ 1 - \prod_{i=1}^{n} \left( 1 - \mu_{\tilde{A}_{Si}}^{2} \right)^{w_{i}} \right]^{1/2}, \prod_{i=1}^{n} \nu_{\tilde{A}_{Si}}^{w_{i}} $$
$$ \left[\prod_{i=1}^{n} \left(1 - \mu_{\tilde{A}_{Si}}^{2}\right)^{w_{i}} - \prod_{i=1}^{n} \left(1 - \mu_{\tilde{A}_{Si}}^{2} - \pi_{\tilde{A}_{Si}}^{2}\right)^{w_{i}}\right]^{1/2}\right\}. (5) $$
The defuzzied (crisp) value of the SFSs is defined as follows [23]:
$$ Def \left(\tilde{A}_s\right) = \left(\mu_{\tilde{A}_s} - \pi_{\tilde{A}_s}\right)^2 - \left(\nu_{\tilde{A}_s} - \pi_{\tilde{A}_s}\right)^2. (6) $$

- e) Step 5. Calculation of final values for the evaluation criteria's weight coefficients: This step calculates the final values of the weight coefficients for the security and privacy properties (w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_n)^T using the fuzzified data from the previous step as follows. - i) Calculate the ratio of the fuzzified data using (7) shown at the bottom of the next page, and (4). $$ \widetilde{E}_{\widetilde{t}}: \ \widetilde{C}_{ij} = \frac{\operatorname{Imp}\widetilde{E1}\left(C1\right)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} \operatorname{Imp}\widetilde{E1}\left(C1\right)} (8) $$
where \widetilde{\mathrm{Imp}(E_{ij}/C_{ij})} represents the fuzzy number of Imp (E_{ij}/C_{ij}), i=1,2,3,\ldots,m, and j=1,2,3,\ldots,n

In this step, one of the fundamental structures of FWZIC is to divide the summed values by a constant. Therefore, (3) is adjusted by using the inverse of the constant as indicated in (9). each criterion should be assigned according to the sum of all the criteria weights for rescaling purposes.
- 2) GRA-TOPSIS Combining With BES Optimization Method: This section presents the ranking strategy for quantifying the evaluation results based on the combination of the GRA-TOPSIS and the BES optimization method. The GRA-TOPSIS method is described by the following steps [28]. - 1) Step1: TOPSIS: In this article, TOPSIS is used to determine the positive NISs. The basic processes of TOPSIS are presented as follows. a) Construct a normalised DM. (11) is a commonly used formula
$$ S_{ij} = x_{ij} / \left(\sum_{i=1}^{k} (x_{ij})^2\right)^{1/2} (11) $$
where x_{ij} is the value of the cell at the i_{th} row (systems) and j_{th} column (the security and privacy properties) intersection in the DM. Let k denote the total number of blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems considered, and m denotes the total number of security and privacy properties. This process produces a normalised DM as follows:
$$ S = \begin{bmatrix} S_{11} & S_{12} & \dots & S_{1m} \\ S_{21} & S_{22} & \dots & S_{2m} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ S_{k1} & S_{k2} & \dots & S_{km} \end{bmatrix} . \tag{12} $$
b) Calculate the weighted matrix. This step can be done by multiplying the set of weights w = w_1, w_2, \dots, w_m calculated by S-FWZIC with the normalised DM, as expressed in
$$ V_{ij} = w_i * S_{ij}, \text{ whwre } w = \begin{bmatrix} w_1 & w_2 & \dots & w_m \end{bmatrix} (13) \begin{bmatrix} w_1 S_{11} & w_2 S_{12} & \dots & w_m S_{1m} \\ w_1 S_{21} & w_2 S_{22} & \dots & w_m S_{2m} \end{bmatrix} (14) $$
$$ = \begin{bmatrix} w_1 S_{11} & w_2 S_{12} & \dots & w_m S_{1m} \\ w_1 S_{21} & w_2 S_{22} & \dots & w_m S_{2m} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ w_1 S_{k1} & w_2 S_{k2} & \dots & w_m S_{km} \end{bmatrix} . \tag{14} $$
c) Determine the PIS and the NIS. The positive ideal A^+ and negative ideal A^- solutions are defined by (15) and (16), respectively, using the weighted normalised DM V.
$$ A^{+} = (v_{1}^{+}, v_{2}^{+}, v_{3}^{+}, \dots, v_{m}^{+})= ((\max v_{ij} | j \in I), (\min v_{ij} | j \in J)) (15) $$
$$ A^{-} = (v_{1}^{-}, v_{2}^{-}, v_{3}^{-}, \dots, v_{m}^{-}) = ((\min v_{ij} | j \in I), (\max v_{ij} | j \in J)) (16) $$
where I represents the benefits criteria; J represents the cost criteria; i = 1, 2, 3, ..., k; j = 1, 2, 3, ..., m.
d) Calculate the Euclidean distance. D_i^+ and D_i^- are calculated for each healthcare Industry 4.0 system in the weighted normalised DM V from the PIS and the NIS through
$$ D_i^{\mp} = \left(\sum_{j=1}^k \left(V_{ij} - v_j^{\mp}\right)^2\right)^{1/2}. (17) $$
2) Step2: GRA: GRA is an alternative method for determining the distance by calculating the grey correlation coefficient matrix of the PIS and the NIS. The mathematical equation of GRA (G_i^{\pm}) is given below. \rho represents the resolution factor and is normally set as 0.5
$$ G_i^{\mp} = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^m r_{ij}^{\mp}}{m} \tag{18} $$
$$ r_{ij}^{\mp} = \frac{\min_{1 \le i \le k} \min_{1 \le j \le m} |v_j^{\mp} - V_{ij}| + \rho \max_{1 \le i \le k} \max_{1 \le j \le m} |v_j^{\mp} - V_{ij}|}{|v_j^{\mp} - V_{ij}| + \rho \max_{1 \le i \le k} \max_{1 \le j \le m} |v_j^{\mp} - V_{ij}|}. (19) $$
- 3) Step3: Hybrid Ranking Method: - a) Calculate the hybrid distance. The hybrid distance is calculated using the following optimization model on the basis of the minimum information entropy principle
$$ \min \mathbf{Z}_{i}^{\mp} = \Sigma_{i=1}^{k} \alpha \cdot H_{i}^{\mp} \ln \left( \frac{H_{i}^{\mp}}{\operatorname{nrm}(D_{i}^{\mp})} \right) + \Sigma_{i=1}^{k} (1 - \alpha) \cdot H_{i}^{\mp} \ln \left( \frac{H_{i}^{\mp}}{\operatorname{nrm}(G_{i}^{\mp})} \right). (20) $$

#### IV. EVALUATION
Sensitivity analysis is used by many researchers, such as [29], to evaluate their results. Sensitivity analysis is performed on the impact of changing the criteria weights on the benchmarking results. Such analysis is essential for determining the robustness of the proposed framework. First, the most significant criterion
was determined by the S-FWZIC method. Then, the impact of altering the criteria weights was examined by generating five scenarios from the relative criteria weights using (22) [30]. The elasticity coefficient (\alpha_c) was used to calculate the relative change of each criterion over the most significant one, and the limit values for altering the weight coefficient of the most significant criterion were identified. Then, the ranks obtained by altering the weights of the criteria in the generated scenarios with the original rank were compared
$$ w_c = (1 - w_s) \times \left(\frac{w_c^o}{W_c^0}\right) = w_c^o - \Delta x \alpha_c \qquad (22) $$
where w_s represents the most significant criteria, w_c^o represents the original weight values calculated by the S-FWZIC method, W_c^0 represents the original weight summation for the changing criteria weight values, and \Delta x represents the range of the changes applied to the weights of the security and privacy criteria which are the limit values of the most significant criteria. Access control (C2 = 0.2070) was identified as the most significant criterion (see Table III) among the six security and privacy criteria. On this basis, the relative weights of each criterion were computed using (22), resulting in five scenarios of altering criteria weights. The elasticity coefficient (\alpha_c) was computed for all the criteria, as given in Table V.
The limit values of the access control criterion are -0.2070 \le \Delta x \leq 0.7930. The defined interval range of the blockchainbased IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems was divided into five sequences, and each of which resulted in the formation of five scenarios and produced new weight values, as given in Table V. The generated weight values were utilized to assess the sensitivity of the benchmarked blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems. The aim is to determine the effect of changing the weights on the final ranking results in each of the five scenarios. Definitely, the importance level of the security and privacy properties plays a critical role in changing the individual rank of the blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems in some scenarios. In the majority of the five scenarios, the power of the proposed integrated method is evident. In the listed scenarios, the first three alternatives (Sys3, Sys5, and Sys9) had the same ranking as S-FWZIC. In the same context, system 14 remained at the fourth rank in all scenarios. Systems 7 and 11 dropped to the seventh rank in S1 and remained stable (rank = 5) in S2-S5. System 12 rose to the ninth rank in S1 and achieved the same ranking results (rank = 11) as S-FWZIC in S2–S5. System 10 maintained the 10th rank in S1 and remained stable (rank = 12) in S2–S4 where it rose to the 11th rank in S5 only. The last three alternatives (Sys1, Sys4, and Sys8) rose to the 12th rank in S1 and had the same ranking result as S-FWZIC in the rest of the scenarios. The ranks of all other systems changed relatively. Finally, the Spearman correlation coefficient (SCC) was utilized to statistically assess the relationship between the results of the five scenarios [30]. In general, the results indicate a high correlation between S-FWZIC and the five scenarios. The SCC values were 0.9 in S1 and 1.0 in the remaining scenarios (S2–S5), with a mean value of 0.964 for all scenarios.
# V. CONCLUSION
This article bridges the existing research gap by solving the complex problem of benchmarking numerous blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems considering multiple evaluation criteria, criteria importance, and data variation. After reviewing the developed MCDM methods, this article proved that the combination of the GRA-TOPSIS and the BES optimization method was the most suitable method for benchmarking the said systems. However, such methods cannot weigh the security and privacy properties, requiring an external method to perform this task. The FWZIC method was the most optimum subjective weighting method for weighting the involved criteria as it successfully addresses the inconsistency issue. To professionally deal with vagueness, hesitancy and uncertainty, this article extended FWZIC under a spherical fuzzy environment. The proposed framework consists of two key phases (i.e., DM identification and development). In the first phase, the intersection of the evaluation criteria and the blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems were achieved to formulate the DM. The second phase, involved the development of the benchmarking framework, illustrating the steps of each MCDM method. After benchmarking the systems, sensitivity analysis was performed to prove the strength of the proposed framework. However, the presented framework has some limitations: the evaluation criteria of blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems were adopted and presented based on two categorical scales only; the importance measurement that reflects each decision-maker preference was not considered; and S-FWZIC was formulated with a single SFS aggregation operator and a single defuzzification method to provide the final weighting and ranking results. Several future directions can be explored: the evaluation criteria of blockchain-based IoT healthcare Industry 4.0 systems might be assessed based on various Likert scales (e.g., 5, 7, and 11 scales); S-FWZIC formulation with other SFS aggregation operators and defuzzification techniques; the use of other fuzzy types with FWZIC, such as Fermatean and fractional orthotriple fuzzy sets, to effectively investigate the uncertainty restriction in other fuzzy sets; the proposed framework can be used to benchmark innovative systems in different categories of healthcare Industry 4.0 systems; and the integration of other MCDM ranking methods with S-FWZIC to investigate new benchmarking results.
